e.t: Adnas is a proper name, also rendered “Athnas.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Nehemiah 12:15. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself supplies no further meaning beyond identifying the individual named there. Its precise significance in that passage comes from the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “impossible”: it describes something that cannot be done, achieved, or brought about. As a verb, it expresses inability rather than naming a person or object. It appears 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of statements. Its first listed occurrence is Genesis 18:14, and its final occurrence is Wisdom 13:16; the precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

“Ever-flowing” describes something that continues to flow without stopping. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe a continuing, inexhaustible flow rather than brief or interrupted movement. The word occurs seven times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Job, Wisdom, Baruch, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the noun or image it describes, but its central idea remains ongoing flow.

This word means “captive”—a person taken and held by others, unable to live freely. It functions as a noun or adjective, identifying someone who has been captured or is in captivity. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, in Genesis 31:26 and Exodus 12:29. Its basic meaning remains focused on a person’s condition as one held captive, while the surrounding verse determines the specific circumstances.

This noun means “change,” referring to an alteration from one state, condition, or arrangement to another. It names the fact or process of things becoming different, rather than describing a person or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the Wisdom of Solomon. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a change or alteration.

This word means “sin” or “fault”: a wrong act or failure that places a person in the wrong. It is a noun used throughout the Greek Old Testament to name wrongdoing, especially in passages dealing with guilt, offerings, confession, and accountability. It occurs 483 times in this corpus, so it is a broad and important term rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes something kept clean, pure, and free from defilement—“untainted” or “undefiled.” It can describe a person or condition regarded as unpolluted rather than corrupted. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs five times, all in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. The English rendering “undefiled” appears in each recorded occurrence, reinforcing the word’s consistent sense of moral or ritual purity. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “forgetfulness of wrong: an amnesty.” It refers to setting aside an offense so that the wrong is no longer held against someone. In ordinary terms, it describes pardon expressed as abandoning a grievance, rather than simply failing to remember an ordinary fact. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the book of Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “slip away”: to leave, depart, or move out of reach. It describes withdrawal or passing away rather than remaining in place. The word occurs 14 times in the deuterocanonical Greek writings represented here, appearing in Wisdom, Sirach, and 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or who is departing and on the surrounding sentence.

This adjective describes something that is “unquestioned” or “impossible to be questioned.” It points to a person, statement, or matter that cannot rightly be challenged or called to account. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Proverbs, so its meaning is established from a small but consistent usage. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but the central idea is freedom from legitimate questioning or accusation.

This adjective describes someone or something as “sung of; famous in song.” It points to a subject remembered or celebrated through singing, especially as worthy of being made known in song. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, at 4 Maccabees 10:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is fame expressed through song or poetic praise.

This verb means “offer” or “begin.” It can describe presenting something, especially as an offering, or starting an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, concentrated mainly in 2 Chronicles, with one occurrence in Proverbs. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on what action or object accompanies it, but its normal range is straightforward: to offer something or to begin doing something.

This Greek LXX verb means “step off” or “step away.” It describes moving away from a place or position, with the surrounding sentence determining the specific situation. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages from Exodus, Job, Proverbs, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. It is especially frequent in Job, where it appears 15 times. Its basic idea remains physical or figurative departure from a point of standing or activity.

Arad, also rendered Arath, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named biblical entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs eight times in the LXX, appearing in Genesis, Numbers, and Judges. Because the supplied lexical information gives the name but not a fuller definition or the identity of the person or place named, its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage. The form is rendered “Arad” in the available translation evidence.

This adjective means “easily numbered” or “few in number.” It describes something limited enough to be counted readily, emphasizing its small or manageable total rather than a particular quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Job, so its normal use is narrowly attested within the LXX corpus. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being counted, but the word itself points to something readily countable or few.

Arouphaios, also rendered Arufeos, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Esther 9:9. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it names a particular person. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s role in the passage.

This adjective describes someone who is irreverent—lacking proper respect toward God and what is holy. It identifies a kind of person or conduct marked by disregard for reverence rather than faithful honor. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, this word occurs 158 times, showing that it is used broadly to describe people or actions opposed to godly respect. Its precise force in any verse is clarified by the surrounding passage.

This noun means “inviolability”: the condition of being protected from violation. It describes a status that others are expected to respect, rather than an action someone performs. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:12. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise force there cannot be described further; its established lexical sense is the protected, inviolable status itself.

Achisamak is a personal name, rendered as “Achisamak” or “Akhisamak.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an object, action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs two times, both in Exodus. The available references place it in Exodus 35:34 and Exodus 37:21, but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so the person’s specific role cannot be explained from the name alone. Its normal function is simply to designate the person called Achisamak.

Basaloth is a proper name, also rendered Vasaloth. It functions as a name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears two times: once in Ezra 2:52 and once in Nehemiah 7:54. The name itself does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond identifying the named entity in those passages. Its exact referent is determined by the surrounding lists and context, which are not included here.

Bezek, also rendered Vezek, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies the named entity represented by this Greek LXX term. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in Judges 1:4–5. The available lexical meaning is therefore the name itself: Bezek or Vezek. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

Booz, also rendered Vooz, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named in several books, especially Ruth, where the name appears frequently. It occurs 32 times across 28 verses in the LXX Old Testament, from Exodus to Isaiah. The name’s exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and narrative, but its basic function remains the same: it identifies the person called Booz.

The word is a proper name for the Galatai, also given as Galate. It identifies a named people or group rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in 1 Maccabees 8:2 and once in 2 Maccabees 8:20. Its exact reference in either passage requires the surrounding verse text for contextual detail.

Gamali is a proper name referring to a person. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears once, in Numbers 13:12. As a personal name, it identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or general idea. The available wording preserves the name as “Gamali,” so its ordinary meaning here is the person’s name itself. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain that individual’s role in the passage.

This noun means “generation”: a group of people belonging to the same period, or the succession of people from one period to another. It can describe human lineage across time and is used broadly in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. This word occurs 202 times in the LXX corpus, beginning in Genesis and continuing through the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise sense in a particular verse depends on how the surrounding passage speaks about time, descendants, or successive generations.

This word means “parent”: a father or mother viewed in relation to a child. It is a noun used for an individual parent or, in the plural, for parents together. In this LXX corpus, it occurs 12 times, including passages in Esther, Proverbs, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books. The central idea is the family relationship between a child and the father or mother identified as the parent. Its precise reference in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “writing” or “letter,” referring to written words or a written message. It is a noun used for something committed to writing, whether understood as writing generally or as a particular letter. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 20 times, with uses spread across books such as Exodus, Joshua, Judges, Isaiah, and Esther. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on whether the surrounding passage focuses on writing itself or on a letter being sent or received.

Dalida is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is also represented as “Thalitha” in the lexical definition. In this Greek LXX corpus, the name occurs ten times, all in Judges 16. The available references show repeated use of the name, while the surrounding verse text is not included here, so the person’s specific role must be understood from the passages themselves.

This noun means “money spent”—an amount used or paid out for a purpose. It points to expenditure rather than to money merely possessed, emphasizing what has been laid out in payment. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both in 2 Maccabees, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the immediate context.

“Dephrōna; Thefrona” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once, in Numbers 34:9. The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain its precise referent or significance. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the name “Dephrōna; Thefrona,” with the passage supplying the context for whom or what it designates.

This verb means “stretch to the uttermost”: to extend something as far as it can go or to reach out fully. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs five times across Psalms, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being extended and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains maximum extension or reach.

This verb means to search through something or examine it closely. It describes an active, careful investigation rather than a quick glance. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both in the book of Wisdom. The word can therefore express the effort to look carefully into something in order to understand, inspect, or discover what is there. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being examined.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Dōdia,” also identified as “Thothia.” It is a personal designation rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Chronicles 27:4 and once in 2 Chronicles 20:37. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the particular person and role in each passage must be understood from those contexts.

This word means “guarantee.” As an adjective, it describes someone or something that serves as a guarantee or provides assurance. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament writings represented here: twice in Sirach and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is dependable assurance—a person or thing presented as security that something will be fulfilled or upheld.

This noun means “gathering in.” It refers to the act of bringing something in or collecting it, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within Exodus 30:13–16. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains an act of gathering or bringing in. The word is therefore best understood as a term describing collection or intake within the passage where it appears.

This verb means “lacking”—being without something needed or expected. It describes a deficiency rather than naming the person or thing that is missing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Zechariah 11:16. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that passage must be understood from the larger context. Its central sense remains the condition of lacking or failing to have something.

This proper name refers to a Hellene, meaning a Greek person or the Greek people. It identifies people associated with Hellenic identity rather than describing an action, feeling, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 13 times, including passages in Isaiah, Daniel, Joel, Zechariah, and the Maccabean books. The precise reference—whether to one person or a wider people—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word refers to burning or blight—a destructive condition associated with burning. It functions as a noun or adjective, naming or describing such an affliction. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, from Leviticus through Daniel. Where an English rendering is recorded, it is rendered “burning,” supporting the central sense of something marked by burning rather than a general feeling or action. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “live amongst,” describing people dwelling or carrying on life among others. It presents living within a community or shared setting rather than being separate from those around them. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:25. The word’s basic sense is therefore the act of residing among a group of people; the surrounding verse determines the specific situation in which that shared living is mentioned.

This verb means to become estranged—to be separated from someone or no longer share a close relationship. It describes a change in relationship rather than merely physical distance. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 12:10. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context, but its central idea is relational separation or alienation.

This noun means “expositor”: a person who explains or makes something understandable. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within three verses in Genesis and Proverbs. Its basic sense points to someone whose role is to give an explanation, especially when meaning is not immediately clear. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being explained in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX adverb means “beyond,” referring to what lies farther on, outside a stated place, boundary, or point of reference. It can describe movement or position beyond something, and its exact force is shaped by the surrounding sentence. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including uses in Genesis, Numbers, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and 1 Samuel. It is a spatial or directional word rather than a name for a person, object, or spiritual quality.

This Greek LXX verb means to “urge on” or “further”—to press someone forward or help a matter advance. It describes active movement toward progress rather than merely observing or waiting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Esther and Proverbs. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains encouraging, hastening, or advancing something. The word is distinct to the Greek LXX corpus represented here.

This word means “vocalize” or “call out”: it describes making one’s voice heard aloud, whether by uttering something or calling to others. As a verb, it focuses on the act of producing a spoken cry or audible expression, rather than on a particular message or emotion. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees 1:23 and once in 3 Maccabees 7:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is being called out in each passage.

This noun means a “trial” or “affliction”—a difficult experience that brings distress, hardship, or testing. It refers to trouble endured by a person rather than to an action performed by someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Job, where it belongs to language describing human suffering and difficulty. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains an experience of severe trial or affliction.

This LXX word denotes the number “6” and is identified with “vav.” It functions as an indeclinable number rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Psalm 118:41. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included, the word’s specific role there cannot be explained further; its established lexical meaning remains the number six.

This Greek word means “seek” or “desire”: to look for something, pursue it, or long for it. It is a verb describing directed action or intention. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly—283 times—so its object and surrounding sentence determine whether the emphasis is searching for something, pursuing a person or goal, or wanting something. The word appears across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books in this Greek corpus, making it a common expression for active seeking or inward desire.

Zoukan, also rendered Zukan, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 1:42. Because it functions as a personal name and no further lexical definition is given, its significance comes from the person named and the surrounding genealogy, not from an ordinary dictionary meaning. The name should therefore be preserved as Zoukan or Zukan when identifying this individual.

This Greek LXX noun means “animal,” referring broadly to a living creature. It can describe ordinary creatures among God’s creation, as in the creation account, and it is also used for living beings in prophetic visions. The word occurs 37 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, so its basic sense covers both earthly animals and visionary living creatures. The surrounding passage determines which kind of creature is intended in a particular verse.

This verb means “wonder”: to respond with amazement, surprise, or admiration at what is seen or heard. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it describes a reaction rather than an object or quality. It occurs 48 times in this LXX corpus, showing regular use for people’s astonishment before striking actions, words, or circumstances. The precise force in any particular verse depends on its surrounding context.

“Thyrsus” is a noun naming a thyrsus, a specific object or emblem referred to by that name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 10:7. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the word’s exact use in that sentence cannot be described safely. Its lexical meaning remains the named item “thyrsus,” while the passage supplies its particular significance.

Iamneia, also called Iamnia, is a proper name for a place. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name used to identify a location in the Greek Old Testament corpus. This name occurs six times, in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees, including references in 1 Maccabees 4:15 and 2 Maccabees 12:40. The precise significance of the place in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and account.

This Greek LXX noun means “sweat,” the moisture produced by the body, especially through exertion, labor, or strain. It names a physical result rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Genesis and twice in 2 and 4 Maccabees. Its ordinary meaning remains straightforward across these occurrences, while the surrounding verse determines why the sweat is being mentioned. The English rendering “sweat” consistently reflects this basic sense.

This word means “hawk” or “falcon,” referring to a bird of prey. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and appears three times, in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Job. The term identifies the bird itself rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the name of this predatory bird.

Itouraios, or Itureos, is a proper name designating someone or something identified by that name. In the Greek Septuagint (LXX), it occurs only once, at 1 Chronicles 5:19. The lexical definition preserves the name rather than describing a quality, action, or abstract idea. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the precise reference of the name in that passage must be understood from the passage itself.

This verb means to “sing hymns continually for sb.” It describes ongoing hymn-singing directed toward a person, rather than a single brief act of singing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 30:21. Its precise emphasis in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is sustained singing of hymns for someone.

This word means “and there,” joining an added statement to a place or situation already being discussed. It combines the connecting force of “and” with the location word “there,” so it can point readers onward to another place or circumstance. In the Greek Old Testament, including its deuterocanonical books, it occurs four times, showing a concise connective expression rather than a broad descriptive term. Its exact emphasis in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to link what follows with a stated location or situation.

Divide means to separate something into distinct portions or groups. It is a verb describing the act of making a division rather than keeping things together. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word occurs four times, in three Psalms passages and once in Joel. Its precise object and force depend on the sentence, but its central idea remains the making of a division. The surrounding passage identifies what is being divided and how that division occurs.

This verb means “strew about”: to spread or scatter something over an area. It describes an action in which things are laid or distributed broadly rather than kept together in one place. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs six times, in Numbers, Job, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being spread and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of scattering or covering an area with something.

This Greek LXX noun means “pillar,” referring to a strong upright support or column. It can describe a structural feature that helps hold up a building or another substantial object. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, across four verses in Judges and 1 Kings. Its basic meaning remains concrete: an upright support, whether mentioned as one pillar or as multiple pillars. The precise significance of a pillar in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description.

Kointos, also rendered Kintos, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:34. The name itself identifies someone, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that person's role or significance in context.

This Greek LXX noun means “judge,” referring to a person who makes decisions or gives judgment. It is used for recognized judges who exercise responsibility among God’s people, and its broader use includes those appointed to judge cases or administer justice. The word occurs 66 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented here, showing that judging is a recurring public responsibility rather than a rare idea. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

Kypros, also rendered Kipros, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a named person, place, or thing in the Greek Old Testament text, while the precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage. This word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in Song of Songs. Its appearances are recorded at Song of Songs 1:14 and 4:13, but the verse text is needed to explain the specific reference in each passage.

Labek; Lavek is a proper name, preserved as an identifying name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore the name itself, not a concept to translate into an English sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Joshua 17:5. The available record does not identify whether the name refers to a person or a location.

This word means “nonsense”—speech regarded as foolish, empty, or without sound sense. It is a noun, naming the kind of talk being dismissed rather than describing a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:11. The surrounding verse is needed to show exactly whose words are being called nonsense and why, but the word itself expresses a judgment that the speech lacks sensible or worthwhile content.

Magaroth is a proper name, rendered as “Magarōth” or “Magaroth.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:59. Without the verse text and surrounding context, its more precise significance cannot be explained beyond its function as a proper name.

This noun means “length of days,” referring to the span or duration of a person’s life. It presents time measured by the days someone has lived, especially when speaking of a long life or continued years. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in Sirach. The word appears in Sirach 1:12, Sirach 1:20, and Sirach 30:22. Those references identify its places of use, while the surrounding verse text is needed to determine the precise emphasis in each passage.

“Man” is a proper name used for the manna given by God as food in the wilderness. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times across four verses, all in Exodus 16. The name identifies the provision Israel received and preserved as a memorial for future generations. Its use is concentrated in the passage describing the manna and its continued availability during Israel’s wilderness journey. This word functions as a name rather than as a general description of any human man.

This adjective means “very glorious,” describing someone or something marked by exceptional glory. It intensifies the idea of being glorious rather than naming an action or object by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: extraordinarily glorious or worthy of great honor.

This Greek LXX noun means “cause of anger”: something that provokes or produces anger. It names the source or occasion of angry feeling rather than the feeling itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 40:4. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise reference in that passage cannot be explained further, but its basic meaning remains clear: an offense, circumstance, or matter that gives rise to anger.

This Greek LXX noun means an instrument or machine: something made or arranged to perform a practical task. It can refer broadly to a device, tool, or piece of equipment rather than to a person or action. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including descriptions of machines and instruments. Its precise reference in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means “5000 dollars,” naming a monetary amount. It appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented in this LXX corpus. Its use is found across passages such as 1 Kings, Ezra, Nehemiah, Ezekiel, and 1 Maccabees, showing that it refers to a stated sum of money rather than an action, person, or quality. The surrounding verse determines what is being valued, paid, given, or counted.

Noemani is a proper name, identifying a person or named group rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It is preserved as the name “Noemani” in the Greek Old Testament and appears once in the LXX, in Numbers 26:44. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s precise identity in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore its function as a distinct biblical name.

This Greek LXX verb means to “guide”—to direct someone along a way or toward a destination. It describes purposeful leadership rather than merely showing a location. The word occurs 43 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with especially frequent use in the Psalms. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what or whom it describes, but its central idea remains directing someone safely or rightly.

This word means “where,” pointing to a place or location. It functions as an adverb or particle, helping identify the setting connected with an action, person, or circumstance. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 23 times, so its basic use is consistent: it directs attention to a particular place, whether physical or understood from the surrounding statement. The exact force of the word in any verse depends on the sentence and passage in which it appears.

Osom is a personal name, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:34. The available lexical identification gives no additional meaning beyond the name itself, so it is best understood as identifying a particular person. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s role or significance in the passage.

This noun refers to sight or the face—the visible appearance or what is seen. It can describe someone’s face or the way something looks, and it may also refer to the act or faculty of seeing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 43 times, with uses ranging from personal appearance to visual observation. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is on a person’s face, outward appearance, or sight itself.

This Greek LXX adverb means “everywhere,” referring broadly to all places or locations rather than one particular place. It describes where something is found, happens, or extends. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus: once in Isaiah and twice in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what the surrounding sentence says is present, occurring, or spreading everywhere.

This noun refers to a lapse or setback—a failure, falling away, or unfortunate reversal. It can describe a person’s departure from what is right or a condition resulting from such a failure. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 16 times, mostly in Ezekiel, and also appears in Job, Psalms, Zechariah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a damaging deviation or fall.

This adjective means “of a leopard.” It identifies something as belonging to, relating to, or characteristic of a leopard, rather than naming the animal itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 9:28. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and the thing being described there.

This noun means “passing,” referring generally to movement by or through a place, or to something passing away. It occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including passages in Genesis, Samuel, Kings, Ezekiel, and Wisdom. The basic idea remains broad rather than describing one particular action: a passing, departure, or transient movement. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording and situation.

This verb means “travel”: to go from one place to another. It describes movement or journeying rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:3, so its wider range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains traveling or proceeding from one location to another.

This Greek LXX noun means “choking”: the condition or act in which breathing is obstructed. It names a physical condition rather than an action someone performs in every use. As a noun, it functions as a name for this condition. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 51:4. The exact force of that occurrence depends on its surrounding verse, but the word’s central meaning remains choking.

This adjective describes someone who is accusing another person in a reproachful or false way. It points to blame expressed as an accusation, especially when the charge is false or presented reproachfully. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in Deuteronomy 22, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word focuses on the manner of accusing rather than simply stating that a disagreement exists. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context.

Remmōth is a proper name, rendered “Remmōth” or “Rhemmoth,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs five times, all within 2 Kings 8–9. The supplied references identify where this name appears, but without verse text they do not establish whether it names a person, place, or other entity. Its precise referent is therefore determined by the surrounding passage.

Saddai, also rendered Saththe, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or name-bearing figure in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Ezekiel 10:5. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific identity and role cannot be stated more precisely; the lexical evidence establishes the name itself, not the larger significance of the passage.

This noun means “sackcloth” or “sack,” referring to coarse material or a sack made from it. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for an actual container or fabric and is also associated with outward signs of mourning, grief, or distress. The word occurs 54 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with “sackcloth” being its usual English rendering. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

Samathiim, also rendered Samathim, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 2:55. The available form preserves the name itself, but does not provide a separate definition or explanation of what the name means. Its significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding genealogy and verse text, rather than on an English lexical meaning supplied here.

“Satrais; Satres” is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:29. The available record identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, so it does not establish the person’s role or significance. Its meaning is therefore best understood as a personal designation preserved in the Greek rendering of this passage.

Seleph, also rendered Selef, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:30. The available wording preserves the person’s name rather than giving an ordinary descriptive meaning such as an action, quality, or object. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further. Its normal function is simply to identify the individual named Seleph or Selef.

Siloam is a proper name, rendered “Silōam” or “Siloam.” It functions as a specific name rather than an ordinary descriptive word, so its meaning is tied to the named person, place, or feature identified by the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Isaiah 8:6. Without the verse text, the name itself can be identified confidently, while its precise significance in that passage must come from its context.

This LXX noun means “staff; cudgel,” referring to a sturdy stick used as a walking staff or a striking implement. Its basic sense is concrete rather than abstract. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, across Exodus, 2 Samuel, and 1 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a staff or club-like object.

Susanna is a proper name—the personal name of a woman in the Greek Septuagint text of Susanna. It identifies the same person wherever it appears, rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. In this corpus, the name occurs three times, all within the book of Susanna. The English rendering is also “Susanna,” preserving it as a personal name rather than translating it into a descriptive word.

This adjective means “standing” or “stationary,” describing something that remains in place rather than moving. It can identify a person or thing as fixed, steady, or unmoving, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek text represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 26:17. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the verse and its context, but its basic sense is something settled in position rather than active movement.

This noun means an “encamped army”—a military force gathered and settled in a camp. It refers to an organized body of soldiers rather than to one individual fighter. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes the army’s presence, its position in camp, or its role in a larger military action.

This Greek LXX verb means “meet.” It describes the act of meeting another person or group, presenting meeting as something someone does rather than as a person, place, or quality. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX material represented here, all in the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the action of meeting.

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “preserve the body by artificial means; embalm.” It describes treating a dead body so that it is preserved rather than left to decay. As a verb, it names an action performed on a body, not a person, object, or feeling. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Epistle of Jeremiah 1:27; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular use there.

This noun means a “bright spot” or “whitened place”—a visibly lighter area or patch. It describes an observable mark rather than an action, feeling, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 13:23. The word’s basic sense is therefore a bright or pale place that can be identified by its appearance. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the description being given there.

This adjective describes something having three teeth or three prongs. It is a concrete descriptive word, used to identify the shape or structure of an object rather than to express an action, emotion, or character trait. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 2:13. The surrounding verse determines exactly what object is being described there, but the word itself points plainly to a three-pronged or three-toothed shape.

This word describes someone who is liable to give account for something—someone answerable for what has been required of them. It functions as a noun, identifying a person under responsibility rather than merely describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 1:23. Its basic emphasis is accountability: an account is due, so the person cannot simply dismiss the matter. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what responsibility is in view.

This verb means “undergird”: to support or strengthen something by fastening or holding it underneath. It describes an action rather than a person or object, and its basic sense is practical support. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:19. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being undergirded there, but the word itself points to providing support beneath something.

This Greek LXX verb means being “fond of money.” It describes a person whose desire or preference is directed toward wealth, emphasizing an attitude toward money rather than merely possessing it. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 10:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: showing an undue or notable attachment to money.

Cheleg, also rendered Kheleg, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person and appears once, in Numbers 26:34. Because it is a personal name, its meaning here is chiefly identification: it distinguishes one individual from others named in the surrounding genealogical record. The name itself does not provide a general teaching or concept apart from the person it names.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Ōsaia” or “Osea.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:32. The name’s precise identity and significance must be understood from that passage and its surrounding context; the name itself does not provide enough information to describe the person’s role or character.
